elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New Section 9.4: "Customer may terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience upon thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor" — both the Agreement and Order Form levels are covered, and the conforming edit to Section 2.1 ("without reduction rights but subject to Section 9.4") removes the retained bar on termination rights that would otherwise contradict it.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: Section 9.4 requires "thirty days' prior written notice to Vendor" — exactly the 30-day written-notice ceiling, with no additional condition or approval.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Section 9.4: "Vendor shall refund, on a pro-rata basis, all prepaid Fees for the period after the effective date of termination." This is an express pro-rata basis (not merely inferred from a post-termination period) and covers all prepaid Fees, curing the narrower "prepaid recurring Fees" language retained in Section 10.2.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Second sentence of Section 9.4: "Vendor has no right to terminate this Agreement or any Order Form for convenience during a committed term." No retained provision (9.1–9.3, 9.5, 27.3) grants Vendor any no-cause exit, so there is no internal inconsistency.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Section 9.4 sets thirty days' notice, which is outside (and better than) the 60–90 day fallback band; the fallback notice parameter is therefore not satisfied on its literal terms.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the redline imposes no early-termination fee, and no retained clause (2.1 take-or-pay as amended, 9.x, 10.2) creates a convenience-exit penalty, so there is no fee to cap.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Exceeded in Customer's favour: Section 9.4 denies Vendor any convenience right during a committed term and no other clause grants one, so Vendor cannot terminate for convenience mid-term at all.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: Vendor has no convenience termination right under the amended Section 9, so no Vendor notice period is engaged.

reasons: All four preferred elements are met in operative text: new Section 9.4 supplies the Customer convenience right over both the Agreement and Order Forms, a 30-day written-notice trigger, an express pro-rata refund of all prepaid Fees for the post-termination period, and an express denial of any Vendor convenience right during a committed term. The position is complete at the preferred level.
Fallback is incomplete only because the 30-day notice sits outside the 60–90 day band; that is irrelevant given the preferred level is fully met.

Minimality holds. The insertion tracks the model language and correctly omits the surplus "in whole or in part" (no partial-termination structure is required by the selected checklist). The only edit outside the new clause is the Section 2.1 conforming change, which is necessary because the retained words "or termination rights" would flatly contradict the new right; the Customer-favourable "without reduction" restriction is preserved rather than deleted.

Intent is preserved: Section 9.4 is placed between 9.3 and 9.5 so numbering and the new Section 2.1 cross-reference both resolve; Sections 9.1–9.3, 9.5 and 10.2 survive without contradiction (9.4's broader all-Fees pro-rata refund supplements, and does not conflict with, the retained recurring-Fees refund in 10.2, which the drafter correctly left intact rather than rewriting).

Minor drafting note only (not a defect requiring repair): "committed term" is used descriptively and is not a capitalised defined term; if the counterparty pushes back, anchor it to the three-year term in Section 8.1 / the take-or-pay period in Section 2.1.
